1:
Ellicott opens with a complaint about the chapter division: the first three verses are wrongly separated from the close of the chapter before, since the narrative is still running parallel to the account in Samuel. He then collects the small departures from that parallel and finds a pattern in them. Where Samuel says David offered the burnt sacrifices, using a different verb, the chronicler's phrasing takes care to make clear that the priests and Levites ministered in the sacrifices. Where Samuel ends the blessing with the divine title Sabaoth, this verse drops it, which Ellicott suggests may mean the title had grown obsolete in the chronicler's day. He also notes that the burnt offering stands in the singular, as if one great holocaust were meant.

What David distributed is genuinely disputed. Ellicott parses each item. The loaf is a round cake, where Samuel uses a rarer word for a sacrificial cake punctured all over. The good piece of flesh is a single Hebrew term found only here and in the parallel, which he takes for a portion of the peace-offering victims, the burnt offerings having been wholly consumed on the altar; the Syriac renders it a portion and the Arabic a slice of flesh, though others make it a measure of wine. The flagon of wine he denies outright, rendering it a raisin-cake, a mass of dried grapes. Clarke has the Targum against him on both counts, which makes the gift the sixth part of an ox and the sixth part of a hin of wine.

On the threefold duty of the singers Ellicott and Delitzsch converge independently. Both insist that "to record" is not a loose synonym for praise but a technical term, and both key it to the superscriptions of the psalms that carry the same word. Ellicott goes further and ties it to the sacrificial rite, making it the chanting that accompanied the burning of the memorial portion of the meat offering; he then distinguishes the other two verbs, thanksgiving being psalms of invocation and confession of benefits received, and praise being hymns of hallelujah such as close the Psalter. Wesley draws the practical inference, that all our rejoicings should express themselves in thanksgivings to him from whom all our comforts are received. Gill supplies a correction about the roster: Asaph is chief of those now appointed, but among the three principal singers Heman was the chief and Asaph next. Ellicott counts the musicians and makes them twelve, which he takes to suggest the twelve tribes, adding that the trumpets are straight clarions and that "continually" is a special term for fixed and regularly recurring services.

Henry reads the day by what the ark had come from and what it was still short of. It had been obscure in a country town, neglected as a despised broken vessel, lodged in a private house by courtesy; now it stood in the royal city where all might resort to it, in a habitation of its own, set in the midst and not crowded into a corner, so that though God's ordinances may be clouded for a time they shall at length shine out of obscurity. Yet this was only a tent, a poor mean dwelling, far short of the temple to come. Henry's verdict on that comparison is the sharpest thing in the passage: David, who pitched a tent for the ark and continued steadfast to it, did far better than Solomon, who built a temple for it and in his latter end turned his back upon it, the church's poorest times having been its purest.
7:
All agree the ode is a cento. Henry sets out the seams: verses 8 to 22 come from Psalm 105, verses 23 to 33 are the whole of Psalm 96 with little variation, verse 34 from Psalm 136, and the last two from the close of Psalm 106. He draws a cheerful conclusion, that we are warranted to do likewise and make up hymns out of David's psalms, a part of one and a part of another. Ellicott draws the opposite conclusion from the same fact and builds four arguments that the ode is a later insertion: the patching is so loose that the seams are quite visible; the Psalter leaves those psalms anonymous, which its editors would hardly have done had they read a clear assertion of Davidic authorship here; the text nowhere says David composed it, and its ideas and language betray a later age; and it makes no specific allusion to the occasion it purports to mark. His reconstruction: no record of the psalms actually sung survived, and some editor supplied the gap from the Psalter.

Delitzsch contradicts the first argument flatly. The hymn, he says, forms a connected and uniform whole, and he lays out its movement to prove it: a summons to praise and seek God's face, a call to remember his wondrous works, the covenant with the patriarchs, the proof of his faithfulness in defending them, the summons to all the world, the homage of the peoples, the rejoicing of nature at his coming to judgment, and a doxology. Ellicott marks the break precisely, where the older psalm would naturally have gone on to Egypt and the Exodus and instead stops dead so a fresh start can be made, and quotes a description of the ode as a mosaic of familiar psalms strung together to express the feelings of the day.

The backbone of Ellicott's case is a running demonstration that this text is secondary to the Psalter's. Where the psalm reads Abraham, this reads seed of Israel, improving the parallelism and probably a correction. Where the psalm says God has remembered his covenant, this turns it into an exhortation, to suit different circumstances. The words "even of the covenant" he would cancel outright; the rhythm at the land of Canaan is marred by a missing particle; a conjunction is prosaic and absent from the psalm; one verse was originally the apodosis of another; and "do no harm against my prophets" is a construction unparalleled elsewhere where the psalm has the ordinary form.

What "first" means in verse 7 divides them three ways. Clarke takes it plainly: David made the psalm on this occasion and gave it to Asaph to be sung. Wesley reads it as first of a series, implying David afterwards delivered many other psalms into their hands. Ellicott renders the verse so that it says nothing about the psalm, only that David then first committed the giving of thanks into the hands of Asaph and his brethren, the duty already described; Delitzsch takes it the same way, to bring out that liturgical singing was then first introduced. Henry alone treats the psalm as composed earlier and now first handed over for the use of the church.

The close of the borrowed portion turns on who the anointed are. Clarke allows the title to the whole people as God's elect as well as to the patriarchs, in whose behalf God had often interfered; Ellicott keeps it narrower, reading the plural of Messiah of Abraham and Sarah as the promised progenitors of kings, and noting that the phrase rendered "do my prophets no harm" is a construction unparalleled elsewhere where the psalm uses the ordinary form.
31: Only one witness speaks to this verse, and what he offers is a note on a translator rather than on the text. Clarke records that the Targum does not let the heavens be glad in their own right but renders the line of the supreme angels, so that the summons to the heavens and the earth becomes a summons to the angelic host above and the inhabitants below. He then notices how the Targumist says it. The word used for angels is not Aramaic at all but the Greek term, written out in Hebrew letters. Clarke draws no conclusion from the observation and leaves it as he found it, but the detail is worth keeping: it shows a paraphrast reaching past his own language for a term he evidently thought clearer, and it dates his idiom by the borrowing.
34:
Ellicott handles the opening formula and the shape it gives the ode. The call to give thanks to the Lord because his mercy endures for ever is one that several of the later psalms use to open with, and he observes that by taking it up here the ode ends with the thought from which it started, since the same verb stood at its beginning. What follows is a petition rather than praise, and the abrupt turn to it raises the question of who is praying.

Gill and Wesley answer the same way and reach the same difficulty. Both hold that David wrote the prayer by a spirit of prophecy, foreseeing that the Israelites would forsake God and be dispersed among the heathen, so that the psalm was made for the use of the church not only in that present time but in future ages. Gill, however, records the alternative without endorsing it: some think these verses were added by Ezra, and he notes in its favour that although a return from the captivity had come in Ezra's day, many still remained in it. That is the same suspicion of a later hand which runs through the treatment of the ode as a whole, surfacing here on two verses.

Clarke takes the petition devotionally instead of historically, and makes a small rule out of it. Because God is addressed here as the God of our salvation, he observes that praying to God under the attribute whose influence we happen to need is itself a help to confidence, and he sets out the pattern in a series: being weak, we appeal to the Almighty for help; being ignorant, to the Father of lights for teaching; being lost, to the merciful God for salvation. Henry keeps the same verse practical in a different direction, taking it as the reminder that in the midst of our praises we must not forget to pray for those servants of God who are in distress, and that since we are members one of another it is not improper, when we mean that God would save them, to say instead that he would save us.
37:
The chapter leaves the ark at Jerusalem and the altar at Gibeon, and Henry cannot account for it. He cannot conceive, he says, why David, who knew the law and was zealous for it, did not either carry the ark to Gibeon where the tabernacle and altar stood or bring them to Zion. His guess is that the curtains of the Mosaic tabernacle were so worn with time and weather as to be unfit either to move or to shelter the ark, and that David would not make all new with the temple so near; whatever the reason, they stayed asunder all his days and neither was neglected. Clarke observes that there were now two high priests and two services but only one ark, Zadok at Gibeon and Abiathar at Jerusalem, and admits we cannot tell how long the Gibeon service continued, though the principal functions were doubtless performed at Jerusalem. Wesley makes the division functional: ordinary sacrifice at Gibeon, extraordinary worship before the ark when God was to be consulted. Henry gives the mechanism: Abiathar was at Jerusalem because he had the breastplate of judgment, consulted before the ark.

Delitzsch explains a silence rather than a statement. It is surprising, he notes, that no priest is named to oversee the sacrifices at the tent of the ark, but the chapter is properly about the sacred music, and Zadok is named only to introduce the singers assigned to Gibeon, so Abiathar may be assumed to have had the oversight at Jerusalem without being named. He also finds a textual fault a verse earlier: the plural in "their brethren" shows that at least one name has dropped out after Obed-edom, and the relation of that clause to the Obed-edom called son of Jeduthun and set among the porters is obscure, the same name appearing elsewhere among the singers and the doorkeepers.

The phrase "musical instruments of God" sets Clarke off into the chapter's longest excursus, against everyone else in it. He first shows that no version takes the Hebrew to mean instruments belonging to God, but instruments employed in the song of God. Then he quotes the Syriac, which he calls remarkable and which turns the clause inside out: these were upright men who did not sing unto God with instruments of music, nor with drums or pipes or cymbals, but sang before the Lord Almighty with a joyous mouth and a pure and holy prayer. Clarke takes that as licence for a series of questions: whether God ever ordained instruments in worship, whether Christ or the apostles sanctioned them, whether musicians are more spiritual than other believers, and whether mere sounds that utter no word or sentiment can be praise at all. His conclusion is that their introduction is antichristian and should be resisted, and that the argument from Jewish use is futile in the extreme applied to Christianity.

Wesley and Henry read the phrase the opposite way, taking the instruments as appropriated to God's worship and not such as were used on other occasions, since between common mirth and holy joy there is a vast difference whose limits must be carefully kept. Henry adds the point Clarke would not grant, that although the ceremonial services were in their own nature inferior to prayer and praise, as types of the mediation of Christ their observance was of great consequence.

On the last verse Ellicott and Delitzsch agree. Both note that the encounter with Michal which follows in Samuel is left out as a domestic matter out of place in a history of sacred institutions, and that the earlier chapter implies the story. Ellicott adds that "returned" is rather went round; Delitzsch that the closing verb means not to greet his house but to bless it, as David had blessed the people. Henry reads it as David resolving to keep up family worship, which public worship must not supersede.
